items.title: WorkBuddy 日活超过 1000 万；曝英伟达未投企业责任险，或因黄仁勋事件遭巨额索赔；DeepSeek 再调整 API 计费 | 极客早知道
items.description: 11 月 18 日消息，据路透社报道，英伟达为公司高管和董事购买了责任保险，最高赔付额度达 9.5 亿美元，但公司自身没有购买通常用于覆盖证券诉讼辩护费用、和解金与判决赔偿的企业责任保险。 这意味着，如果围绕黄仁勋突然辞去 CEO 职务引发的诉讼最终胜诉，涉及股价暴跌的赔偿需要由公司自行承担。英伟达目前持有超过 500 亿美元现金储备。自 11 月 8 日黄仁勋承认对妻子不忠以来，针对英伟达及相关人员的诉讼至少已有两起，其中包括一名个人股东在旧金山联邦法院提起的拟议集体诉讼，指控公司及黄仁勋涉嫌证券欺诈、误导投资者。

items.description: OpenAI 正式发布 GPT-6.2 Astra 和 GPT-6.2 Sol 两款模型，重点提升专业任务、Coding、电脑操作和执行效率，并降低部分使用成本。新模型将应用于 ChatGPT Work、Codex 和 API。 其中，Astra 面向复杂编程和专业工作，Sol 则更强调日常多模态任务及工具使用。

items.title: 最大规模具身大模型挑战赛落幕，48 小时真机总决赛比出了什么？

items.title: AI，没有抛弃小城商家
items.description: 从最开始谈技术，讲参数有多大，算得有多快，跑分超过多少人，慢慢转变为讲落地，讲 AI 怎么一分钟生成商业计划书，怎么给被生活困扰的人们出情绪价值满满的建议。 走出实验室，AI 下一站在哪里？这背后，是一段讲了一半的「AI 平权」故事。前面讲的这一半，是消费者：普通人用 AI 获取信息、写方案、做攻略。还有没讲完的一半，在经营者那里——对小店老板来说，AI 平不平权，从来不是能不能跟它聊天，而是它能不能帮自己管钱、管货、管客流。

items.title: 全村希望，千问 4 Max 正式发布，2.4 万亿参数模型「进厂打工」
items.description: 11 月 16 日，阿里千问正式发布新一代旗舰模型 Qwen4-Max。就在五天前，它的预览版 qwen4-max-preview 刚在 Token Plan 里低调露过面，今天正式版直接亮出了完整底牌。 新模型依然维持着 2.4 万亿（2.4T）的主干总参数规模，原生支持文本、图像和视频输入，上下文窗口拉到了 100 万 Token。不过比参数表更显眼的，是官方同时给出的一笔账单：在模拟真实工作场景的评测里，千问 4 Max 跑完单个任务的平均费用， 从上一代的 26.58 元降到了 11.16 元，直接砍掉 58% 。

items.title: OpenAI 和 Meta 联手，打通了 Agent 商业「最后一公里」
items.description: 美国时间 2026 年 11 月 13 日，两家公司两场发布会同天发生。一边是企业级对话式智能体公司 Sierra 联合 Meta 正式发布个 人代理协议 Poppy v1.0，解决助手怎么「进门」的问题 ；另一边是 OpenAI 推出面向个人助手 dots 的 ChatGPT Wallet， 解决助手怎么「付钱」的问题 。 同一天打通进门和结账，本身就足够耐人寻味。更值得留意的，是站在两套方案背后的同一批名字。Visa 和 Mastercard 同时出现在两边的名单里，Shopify、Stripe 这些掌管电商与支付基础设施的公司，则站在 Poppy 的核心伙伴之列。

items.title: 接入多款第三方模型，豆包工作也模型自由了
items.description: 头图来源：豆包工作官网 豆包工作也模型自由了。 11 月 12 日，豆包工作宣布接入 Kimi K3.1 Pro、GLM 5.3、DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 等多款第三方模型，支持用户按需选型完成任务。同步在模型选择页面标注各模型额度消耗倍率，倍率越低消耗越少，便于用户结合任务需求与使用成本做决策。 同时平台推出两项限时优惠：一是工作日及节假日的指定时段内，使用活动模型可享受额度消耗折扣；二是豆包 2.1 Lite、DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 两款模型限时下调额度消耗倍率，同等任务消耗额度更少。 一、补全多模型，解决「有的选」 本轮更新中，豆包工作一次性接入 Kimi 3.1 Pro、GLM 5.3、DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 三款第三方模型，进一步补齐了模型能力矩阵。 具体来看，三款模型各有侧重，可以分别对应企业不同层级的工作场景：Kimi 3.1 Pro 主打百万字级超长上下文处理能力；GLM 5.3 侧重中文语言理解与生成；DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 以高响应速度和高性价比为核心，定位轻量日常任务。 加上此前已经开放的第三方模型，以及字节跳动自研的豆包 2.1、豆包 2.1 Lite 等主力模型，豆包工作已经具备了覆盖「高端能力型、均衡通用型、轻量效率型」三个层级的模型矩阵。 不同能力、不同定价的模型相互补充，基本可以覆盖企业从核心复杂任务到日常基础工作的多场景 AI 需求。 事实上，豆包工作此前就已向企业客户开放第三方模型能力。本轮扩容并非单纯的数量叠加，而是基于企业真实工作流的场景化补全。 图片来源：豆包工作官网 此外，我们也注意到，豆包工作本次同步更新了 LOGO，大家熟悉的豆包形象就此「持证上岗」，进入了专业办公场景。 二、额度倍率透明化，把成本决策权交还给用户 如果说模型扩容是解决「有没有得选」的问题，那么额度消耗倍率的透明化标注，则是解决「选得明不明白」的问题。 在当前的企业级 AI 市场，成本不透明是很多企业的普遍困扰。不同模型的计费规则各不相同，有的按输入输出 token 计费，有的按调用次数收费，不同单位之间换算复杂，普通用户很难快速判断一款模型的实际使用成本。 很多团队在使用过程中，往往难以预估单任务开销，直到账单出来才发现超出预算，也很难追溯成本的具体构成。 针对这一问题，豆包工作在模型选择页面统一标注了各模型的额度消耗倍率—— 倍率系数越低，同等任务消耗的平台额度越少。所有模型的消耗标准统一到同一额度体系下，用户选型时可直观对比成本差异，结合任务优先级与预算快速决策，也便于企业做部门的成本管控。 在简单小额任务免费的基础上，豆包工作同步上线两项限时优惠政策，进一步压低使用成本： 一是指定时段折扣，工作日及节假日的优惠时段内使用活动模型，可享受额度消耗减免，兼顾用户成本与平台算力效率； 二是高频模型降倍率，针对豆包 2.1 Lite 与 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 两款日常高频使用的轻量模型，限时下调消耗倍率，同等任务消耗更少，提升全员日常使用的额度耐用性。 当大模型的基础能力逐渐拉平，如何帮企业把 AI 用起来、用得划算，才是落地的关键。从提供单一模型，到提供多模型矩阵；从黑盒计费，到透明化成本管控，豆包工作的产品迭代路径，契合了企业 AI 从「尝鲜」到「常态化生产工具」的转变趋势。 再往前看一步，当模型足够多、倍率足够清晰，用户可能连「选哪个模型」都不需要亲自操心，平台基于任务类型自动路由、智能调度，会成为下一个自然的产品方向。

items.title: 苹果突然永久关闭官方「支持社区」；字节即将推出个人 AI 助手；华为新品牌星芒 OSTA 曝光 | 极客早知道
items.description: 11 月 11 日，苹果官网突然宣布，Apple 支持社区将于 2026 年 11 月 20 日永久关闭。即日起，社区将不再接受新帖子，并转为只读模式。用户仍可前往官方 Apple 支持网站，获取值得信赖的指导和帮助。 苹果公告称，我们衷心感谢各位社区成员一直以来贡献宝贵的时间和专业知识，帮助其他用户解决 Apple 产品使用中遇到的问题。（来源：新浪科技）

items.title: 当美国无法建设数据中心，会对 AI 产生怎样的冲击
items.description: 2026 年 11 月 4 日，美国中期选举结果落定后的第二天上午，OpenAI 的高管们坐到了一起。 据外媒援引知情人士的消息，他们讨论的是要不要重设 2027 年的数据中心容量预期。讨论还没有形成决定，但焦虑已经摆上了台面。

items.title: Anthropic 启动 IPO 路演，创始人将套现 17.5 亿美元；谷歌最强 AI 模型正式开放；任天堂招新：经典游戏保存员
items.description: 11 月 11 日消息，英伟达发布公告，宣布已聘请美国前联邦检察官金正贤（Joon H. Kim）及其所在的律师事务所 Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz，负责开展一项全面、独立的调查。 此前，英伟达董事会表示，鉴于近期有关公司创始人兼 CEO 黄仁勋可能成为外国情报机构目标的报道，董事会决定启动独立调查。董事会将成立由独立董事组成的委员会，并在外部独立法律顾问协助下监督调查。

items.title: 千问办公押注 Team Agent，企业 AI 的流水线时刻真的来了
items.description: 传说，光明之神巴德尔梦见自己将死，于是，巴德尔的母亲弗丽嘉遍走世间，令万物立下了绝不伤害他的誓言。众神也因此放下心来，甚至还发明了一种新的消遣：轮番向巴德尔投掷武器和石块，看着他毫发无损，来确定他们已经战胜了预言。直到一小枝被遗漏的槲寄生投向巴德尔。光明之神轰然倒下，诸神的黄昏由此拉开序章。 这是北欧神话中巴德尔之死的故事。危险早已被预见，人们也采取了行动，却仍然自欺欺人，把一次次看似成功的演示，当成了问题已经解决的证明 。

items.title: ChatGPT 占全球 AI 聊天流量超 81%；iOS 27.3 曝光 Siri「个人记忆系统」；传玛莎拉蒂+尊界合作新车曝光｜极客早知道
items.description: 11 月 10 日消息， Anthropic 昨日（11 月 9 日）官宣推出 Claude Fable 5.2 和 Claude Mythos 5.2， 两款模型基于同一底层模型，前者面向普通用户并内置网络安全与生物安全防护，后者则面向通过审核的网络安全和生命科学机构开放，用于高风险的专业应用。 定价方面，Claude Fable 5.2 每 100 万词元（Token）输入费用为 8 美元（IT 之家注：现汇率约合 53.4 元人民币），每 100 万词元（Token）输出费用为 40 美元（现汇率约合 267.2 元人民币）。作为对比，Claude Fable 5.1 的每 100 万词元输入 / 输出价格分别为 10 美元（现汇率约合 66.8 元人民币）和 50 美元（现汇率约合 334 元人民币）， 按此计算 5.2 版本的 API 调用费用下调 20%。

items.title: 田渊栋创业合伙人：通往 AGI 最快的路，只能是 AI 造 AI | CoRL 2026
items.description: 11 月 12 日，CoRL 2026 最后一天。主会已经结束，32 场 Workshop 密集进行，其中一场聚焦持续自进化（Continually Self-Improving），英属哥伦比亚大学教授、Uber AI Labs 创始成员 Jeff Clune 受邀来做分享。 今年 5 月，田渊栋（前 Meta FAIR 研究总监、ELF OpenGo 主导者）与其他七位联合创始人创办 Recursive Superintelligence，Jeff Clune 是其中一位。这家公司首轮融资 6.5 亿美元，投后估值 46.5 亿美元，谷歌 GV 与 Greycroft 联合领投，英伟达和 AMD 两大算力巨头同时押注。

items.title: Google 杀入 Jev 核心赛道：Gemini Decision 1 五项基准领先两项落后
items.description: 刚刚，谷歌发布 Gemini Decision 1，正式向 两个月前引爆决策模型品类的 TypeSafe Jev发起挑战。 和 Jev 一样，这款模型不生成任何文本，只计算供程序直接驱动 Agent 执行的候选项概率和置信度，不需要逐 Token 生成答案，连输出 Token 费用也省了。

items.title: 黄仁勋「每天都在用」的 Perplexity 开始重构 Attention，把「判断」做成了一个独立模型
items.description: Perplexity 这次直接改了模型处理判断任务的方式： 同一份上下文可以同时交给多个问题使用，模型只需进行一次前向传播，就能输出各个问题的答案概率。 过去需要反复调用 LLM、生成文本、解析结果的流程，现在可以收敛到一次模型计算中。 为了让多个问题共享计算时不互相干扰，Perplexity 还重新设计了 Attention 机制，让共享状态读取全部问题，同时限制问题之间直接交换信息。v1.3 进一步加入 Locate 能力，可以根据字段描述直接定位原文跨度，将判断与文本抽取整合进同一套架构。

items.title: 对话西湖大学于开丞：通用语言模型再强，物理世界也「等不起」
items.description: 这个语言模型没有为机器人做任何专项训练，就在 42 项操作任务上拿下平均成功率第一，反超 40 个公开机器人策略。 世界模型这张牌桌，被搅了局 。“语言模型是不是连世界模型的活都能干了？”这个问题被重新摆上桌面。

items.title: AI 带来的新生意｜稀土掘金 X-Lab 年度大会招募开启
items.description: 稀土掘金 X-Lab 年度大会启动作品征集，聚焦「AI 带来的新生意」 2026 年 12 月 26 日（周六），由稀土掘金 X-Lab 主办的年度大会将在深圳举行。 作品展示申请、观众报名与实践分享征集现已开放。 大会上午设主会场主题演讲，下午安排并行分场讨论与作品展示交流。 大会将设置作品展示与交流区。作者可以演示产品和原型，观察别人如何理解、如何操作，听到具体的使用反馈；观众可以上手体验，也可以带着自己的任务，与作者讨论产品是否适合实际需求。 入选项目可获得现场展示席位、活动作品介绍与宣传曝光机会 ，并与开发者、潜在用户和合作伙伴面对面交流。项目演示及交流安排将结合征集情况陆续公布。 外地团队可申请差旅支持 ，具体范围、条件与额度在入选后单独沟通。无论是创意、Demo，还是已经有人在用的产品，都欢迎带到现场交流，让讨论从「你做了什么」走向「它能为谁解决什么问题」。 欢迎个人开发者与小团队申请展示 AI 相关的产品、工具、服务或创作项目。应用 AI 的产品、借助 AI 开发的作品，以及用 AI 完成关键生产环节的内容项目，都可以参与征集。早期原型也欢迎申请，不要求已经商业化； 作品需可运行、可演示或可交互 ，作者或核心成员能够到场交流。可登录稀土掘金官网大会主页报名， 申请前，请先在掘金作品广场发布作品页，再提交作品展示申请，并填写对应链接。 上午主会场将邀请一线实践者，围绕 AI 应用机会与产品商业化分享亲历的经验。新机会长在哪些老需求里？有些需求一直存在，只是过去服务起来太贵、太难；有些产品原本只能服务少数人，现在有机会触达更多用户；也有一些成熟市场，正在出现新的产品、体验和交付方式。通过具体案例，看清 AI 改变了其中的哪一步：用户原来怎么解决问题，新的解法为什么值得尝试，又有哪些使用结果支持这个判断。 大会也将讨论从一个 Demo 到第一个付款用户的过程：第一个愿意试用的人从哪里来？最初的需求判断有没有错？第一个付费用户为什么愿意买单？交付之后，产品又做了哪些调整？这一方向将围绕需求验证、首笔订单与交付经验展开。有效的做法值得分享，没有成功的尝试同样值得复盘。对于正在打磨产品的人，一次真实取舍，往往比一套完整的方法论更能帮助判断下一步。 下午将围绕产品商业化、增长和 Agent 产品等方向开展并行交流。产品商业化专场讨论需求取舍、产品体验、定价与交付；增长专场围绕冷启动、渠道选择、用户反馈、留存与付费转化，邀请实践者讲清哪些有效、哪些没有奏效；Agent 专场讨论场景选择、任务边界、结果验证与人工接管，以及哪里应该自动完成、哪里需要询问用户。分场内容将结合征集案例与合作伙伴共创陆续公布。 如果你正在用 AI 做产品、探索新的创作方式，或希望判断某个工具能否解决工作与生活中的实际问题，欢迎作为观众报名。你可以听一线经验、体验作品，也可以向作者提问，与同行交流自己的尝试。活动免费报名，采用审核制；详细地址随参会确认通知公布。可登录稀土掘金官网大会主页报名。 如果你亲历过 AI 产品开发、增长、Agent 设计或商业交付，欢迎提交分享主题。可以是一项有效的做法、一次没有成功的尝试，也可以是仍在寻找答案的具体问题。初次提交提供一个主题、150—300 字提纲及相关案例材料即可，不便公开的客户名称、收入和订单信息可脱敏处理。我们更关心问题是怎样发生的、你做过哪些选择、结果和预期有什么不同。可登录稀土掘金官网大会主页报名。 开发者社区、创作者组织、AI 产品与服务平台、园区及有具体应用需求的伙伴，也欢迎参与分场共创、推荐嘉宾与作品、带来试用资源或真实需求。合作意向请发送至 bd@xitu.io，简要介绍机构与希望参与的方式。稀土掘金 X-Lab 通过线上作品广场与线下活动，让作品被看见，让创造者获得交流与反馈。带上你的作品、经验或问题，和我们一起寻找 AI 带来的新生意。 雷峰网 雷峰网

items.title: 百图生科正式发布AI药物安全性评价系统，从虚拟细胞走向虚拟猴，为药物研发带来全新助力
items.description: 11月19日，百图生科正式发布AI药物安全性评价系统（以下简称“AI安评系统”），将虚拟细胞模型、毒性预测能力与非临床安全性评价服务相结合，依托“虚拟猴”等安全性预测模型，将AI预测从细胞层面延伸至动物体内。 AI安评系统正式对外发布，也标志着公司的虚拟细胞能力开始从公开评测走向真实药物研发流程，从细胞状态预测进一步向赋能动物体内安全性评价延伸，帮助研发团队在投入动物实验前，判断哪些候选分子值得优先推进、哪些风险需要优先验证。

items.title: AI4S青年志②丨赋澈生物王子龙：实验室里的「企业家」
items.description: 【编者按】AI4S有时给人“雷声大雨点小”之感，是因为不少人把AI当成了目的本身，拿着锤子满世界找钉子，对科研周期与商业回报的错配却无知无觉。“AI4S青年志”第二篇，我们关注一个可能破解AI4S落地困局的样本。 但当《Nature Biotechnology》的编辑们打开一篇来自加州大学伯克利分校的投稿时，他们很快意识到，2-4位远远不够。为了覆盖这篇论文涉及的每一个学科，编辑们前后邀请的审稿人数量已经来到了两位数。

items.title: AI 已经进入企业，为什么组织还没有进化？
items.description: 最近与AI圈子的人聊，普遍谈到一个点，人已经接受AI提效，但企业还没准备好。 （雷峰网雷峰网雷峰网） 一边是员工已经在用agent 干活、甚至开始自己搭小系统；另一边是公司的KPI、审批链、汇报节奏，还按着三年前的样子在转。

items.title: 纽娲机器人创始人杨睿刚：自动驾驶踩过的数据坑，机器人还会再踩一遍丨物理 AI 50 人
items.description: 在此之前，他曾在美国高校研究三维视觉，后来加入百度研究院，负责机器人与自动驾驶实验室，又担任嬴彻科技CTO，推动自动驾驶重卡前装量产。从研究算法到让几十吨重的卡车真正跑上高速公路，他经历了自动驾驶从技术探索走向商业化的过程。 2024年，杨睿刚开始筹备第二次创业。彼时，人形机器人已经成为具身智能行业最受关注的方向，他也接触过相关创业机会，但最终选择了一个看起来没那么性感的场景：社区末端配送。

items.title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
items.description: Jensen Huang has resigned from Nvidia following an affair, which could have ramifications for national security as the U.S. and China race to develop the most advanced AI infrastructure.

items.title: Anthropic’s IPO could deliver $156 billion to charity
items.description: At a stock price of $95, the frontier lab's Public Benefit Foundation, its employee donations, and the company's match tot up to $156 billion.

items.title: Google gives Gemini the ability to use your Mac for you
items.description: Google's latest update to Gemini brings an AI agent to the Mac that can organize files, fill out forms, and tackle multistep workflows.

items.description: In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn't belong to them.

items.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
items.description: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running: I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches. Tags: sandboxing…

items.title: llm 0.37.3
items.description: Release: llm 0.37.3 A bug fix release for LLM , mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software. Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1 , which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code . Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL: select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) Returns this: {"a":[1]} But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this: {"a":"[1]"} According to D. Richard Hipp : That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug. The workaround looks like this: select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1)))) Tags: sqlite , ai , webassembly , d-richard-hipp , generative-ai , llms , llm

items.title: Gemini Decisions API
items.description: Gemini Decisions API Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million. Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. I tested it against video by passing these questions to it along with my Yonkers stomping robot video file: dragon: Does this video have a dragon in it? robot: Does this video have a robot in it? france: Is this video set in France? usa: Is this video set in the USA? Jev and OpenAI both return 1.0 or 0.0 for yes/no questions, but Gemini insists on being a little less confident than that: { "dragon" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.04976021841520312 }, "robot" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9234055387792485 }, "france" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.08329171353166241 }, "usa" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9230459995157706 } } Via Hacker News Tags: ai , generative-ai , gemini , llm-release , jev , decision-models

items.title: aws-emulator
items.description: aws-emulator Finally, an official emulator from AWS to run tests against a local clone of their many different services without having to provision a paid API key to do so. It's written in Rust by a huge swarm of agents - 29,684 commits in the first three weeks of the project. Swaminathan (Swami) Sivasubramanian wrote about how it came to be in a guest post on Werner Vogels' blog. It currently requires Docker to run on macOS or Windows. items.title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
items.description: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or…

items.title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
items.description: Claude Fable 5.2 pays close attention to who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model tended to add to the existing structure when the prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, even when that duplicated existing code. When the prompt said the code base was the model’s own, it often consolidated duplicated code and sometimes made related fixes without being asked. If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you. The ownership sentence makes the model much more likely to consolidate duplicated code into one shared function. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model consolidated duplicated code in under 10 percent of runs without the sentence and in about 75 percent of runs with it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation Tags: ai , prompt-engineering , generative-ai , llms , anthropic , claude-mythos-fable

It just isn't worth it to anyone. And agents aren't real and they might not be being used the way that anyone wants them to yet. All these companies are spending more than they're making on these products. Refrigerators holding blood storage in Europe are being hacked. The costs are too high. The benefits are not real. And if you connect that to corruption, you're like, in order to impose these costs on me, these CEOs are in the White House shaking Trump's hand, renaming it to the Gulf of America, paying for this ballroom that we don't want. items.title: Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement
items.description: The concept of recursive self-improvement (RSI) dates back to I. J. Good (1965) , where he defined an “ultraintelligent machine” as a system that can surpass humans in all intellectual activities and design better machines to improve itself. Yudkowsky (2008) used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” for a specific feedback loop: an AI uses its current intelligence to improve the cognitive machinery that produces its intelligence. This feedback loop in modern AI may indicate the model rewriting its own weights directly, or more broadly the model improves the training pipeline and the deployment system , which in turn enables a better successor model with improved performance across economically valuable tasks. The speed of research development in AI has been shown to drastically accelerated in frontier labs ( Anthropic ; OpenAI ).

items.title: Scaling Laws, Carefully
items.description: Scaling laws are one of the most critical empirical findings in deep learning. The observation is simple in form: the training loss $L$ decreases predictably as we scale up model size $N$, dataset size $D$, and compute $C$, following a power-law curve, which appears as a straight line on a log-log plot. We can view scaling laws as a framework for describing the relationship between compute, loss, model size and data; at its core, it is about how to allocate precious compute optimally between $N$ and $D$.

items.title: Why We Think
items.description: Special thanks to John Schulman for a lot of super valuable feedback and direct edits on this post. Test time compute ( Graves et al. 2016 , Ling, et al. 2017 , Cobbe et al. 2021 ) and Chain-of-thought (CoT) ( Wei et al. 2022 , Nye et al. 2021 ), have led to significant improvements in model performance, while raising many research questions. This post aims to review recent developments in how to effectively use test-time compute (i.e. “thinking time”) and why it helps.

items.title: Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning
items.description: Reward hacking occurs when a reinforcement learning (RL) agent exploits flaws or ambiguities in the reward function to achieve high rewards, without genuinely learning or completing the intended task. Reward hacking exists because RL environments are often imperfect, and it is fundamentally challenging to accurately specify a reward function. With the rise of language models generalizing to a broad spectrum of tasks and RLHF becomes a de facto method for alignment training, reward hacking in RL training of language models has become a critical practical challenge. Instances where the model learns to modify unit tests to pass coding tasks, or where responses contain biases that mimic a user’s preference, are pretty concerning and are likely one of the major blockers for real-world deployment of more autonomous use cases of AI models.

items.title: Extrinsic Hallucinations in LLMs
items.description: Hallucination in large language models usually refers to the model generating unfaithful, fabricated, inconsistent, or nonsensical content. As a term, hallucination has been somewhat generalized to cases when the model makes mistakes. Here, I would like to narrow down the problem of hallucination to cases where the model output is fabricated and not grounded by either the provided context or world knowledge. There are two types of hallucination: In-context hallucination: The model output should be consistent with the source content in context. Extrinsic hallucination: The model output should be grounded by the pre-training dataset. However, given the size of the pre-training dataset, it is too expensive to retrieve and identify conflicts per generation. If we consider the pre-training data corpus as a proxy for world knowledge, we essentially try to ensure the model output is factual and verifiable by external world knowledge. Equally importantly, when the model does not know about a fact, it should say so. This post focuses on extrinsic hallucination. To avoid hallucination, LLMs need to be (1) factual and (2) acknowledge not knowing the answer when applicable.

items.title: Diffusion Models for Video Generation
items.description: Diffusion models have demonstrated strong results on image synthesis in past years. Now the research community has started working on a harder task—using it for video generation. The task itself is a superset of the image case, since an image is a video of 1 frame, and it is much more challenging because: It has extra requirements on temporal consistency across frames in time, which naturally demands more world knowledge to be encoded into the model. In comparison to text or images, it is more difficult to collect large amounts of high-quality, high-dimensional video data, let along text-video pairs. 🥑 Required Pre-read: Please make sure you have read the previous blog on “What are Diffusion Models?” for image generation before continue here.

items.title: Thinking about High-Quality Human Data
items.description: [Special thank you to Ian Kivlichan for many useful pointers (E.g. the 100+ year old Nature paper “Vox populi”) and nice feedback. 🙏 ] High-quality data is the fuel for modern data deep learning model training. Most of the task-specific labeled data comes from human annotation, such as classification task or RLHF labeling (which can be constructed as classification format) for LLM alignment training. Lots of ML techniques in the post can help with data quality, but fundamentally human data collection involves attention to details and careful execution. The community knows the value of high quality data, but somehow we have this subtle impression that “Everyone wants to do the model work, not the data work” ( Sambasivan et al. 2021 ).

items.title: Adversarial Attacks on LLMs
items.description: The use of large language models in the real world has strongly accelerated by the launch of ChatGPT. We (including my team at OpenAI, shoutout to them) have invested a lot of effort to build default safe behavior into the model during the alignment process (e.g. via RLHF ). However, adversarial attacks or jailbreak prompts could potentially trigger the model to output something undesired. A large body of ground work on adversarial attacks is on images, and differently it operates in the continuous, high-dimensional space. Attacks for discrete data like text have been considered to be a lot more challenging, due to lack of direct gradient signals. My past post on Controllable Text Generation is quite relevant to this topic, as attacking LLMs is essentially to control the model to output a certain type of (unsafe) content.

items.title: LLM Powered Autonomous Agents
items.description: Building agents with LLM (large language model) as its core controller is a cool concept. Several proof-of-concepts demos, such as AutoGPT , GPT-Engineer and BabyAGI , serve as inspiring examples. The potentiality of LLM extends beyond generating well-written copies, stories, essays and programs; it can be framed as a powerful general problem solver. Agent System Overview In a LLM-powered autonomous agent system, LLM functions as the agent’s brain, complemented by several key components: Planning Subgoal and decomposition: The agent breaks down large tasks into smaller, manageable subgoals, enabling efficient handling of complex tasks. Reflection and refinement: The agent can do self-criticism and self-reflection over past actions, learn from mistakes and refine them for future steps, thereby improving the quality of final results. Memory Short-term memory: I would consider all the in-context learning (See Prompt Engineering ) as utilizing short-term memory of the model to learn. Long-term memory: This provides the agent with the capability to retain and recall (infinite) information over extended periods, often by leveraging an external vector store and fast retrieval. Tool use The agent learns to call external APIs for extra information that is missing from the model weights (often hard to change after pre-training), including current information, code execution capability, access to proprietary information sources and more. Overview of a LLM-powered autonomous agent system. Component One: Planning A complicated task usually involves many steps. An agent needs to know what they are and plan ahead.

items.title: Prompt Engineering
items.description: Prompt Engineering , also known as In-Context Prompting , refers to methods for how to communicate with LLM to steer its behavior for desired outcomes without updating the model weights. It is an empirical science and the effect of prompt engineering methods can vary a lot among models, thus requiring heavy experimentation and heuristics. This post only focuses on prompt engineering for autoregressive language models, so nothing with Cloze tests, image generation or multimodality models. At its core, the goal of prompt engineering is about alignment and model steerability. Check my previous post on controllable text generation.

Version 2.0 is a superset of the old version, about twice the length. The Transformer (which will be referred to as “vanilla Transformer” to distinguish it from other enhanced versions; Vaswani, et al., 2017 ) model has an encoder-decoder architecture, as commonly used in many NMT models. Later simplified Transformer was shown to achieve great performance in language modeling tasks, like in encoder-only BERT or decoder-only GPT .

items.title: Some Math behind Neural Tangent Kernel
items.description: Neural networks are well known to be over-parameterized and can often easily fit data with near-zero training loss with decent generalization performance on test dataset. Although all these parameters are initialized at random, the optimization process can consistently lead to similarly good outcomes. And this is true even when the number of model parameters exceeds the number of training data points. Neural tangent kernel (NTK) ( Jacot et al. 2018 ) is a kernel to explain the evolution of neural networks during training via gradient descent. It leads to great insights into why neural networks with enough width can consistently converge to a global minimum when trained to minimize an empirical loss. In the post, we will do a deep dive into the motivation and definition of NTK, as well as the proof of a deterministic convergence at different initializations of neural networks with infinite width by characterizing NTK in such a setting.

items.title: Generalized Visual Language Models
items.description: Processing images to generate text, such as image captioning and visual question-answering, has been studied for years. Traditionally such systems rely on an object detection network as a vision encoder to capture visual features and then produce text via a text decoder. Given a large amount of existing literature, in this post, I would like to only focus on one approach for solving vision language tasks, which is to extend pre-trained generalized language models to be capable of consuming visual signals .

items.title: Learning with not Enough Data Part 3: Data Generation
items.description: Here comes the Part 3 on learning with not enough data (Previous: Part 1 and Part 2 ). Let’s consider two approaches for generating synthetic data for training. Augmented data . Given a set of existing training samples, we can apply a variety of augmentation, distortion and transformation to derive new data points without losing the key attributes. We have covered a bunch of augmentation methods on text and images in a previous post on contrastive learning. For the sake of post completeness, I duplicate the section on data augmentation here with some edits. New data . Given few or even no data points, we can rely on powerful pretrained models to generate a number of new data points. This is especially true in recent years given the fast progress in large pretrained language models (LM) . Few shot prompting is shown to be effective for LM to learn within context without extra training. Data Augmentation The goal of data augmentation is to modify the input format (e.g. text wording, visual appearance) while the semantic meaning stays unchanged.

items.title: Agents
items.description: Intelligent agents are considered by many to be the ultimate goal of AI. The classic book by Stuart Russell and Peter Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (Prentice Hall, 1995), defines the field of AI research as “ the study and design of rational agents. ” The unprecedented capabilities of foundation models have opened the door to agentic applications that were previously unimaginable. These new capabilities make it finally possible to develop autonomous, intelligent agents to act as our assistants, coworkers, and coaches. They can help us create a website, gather data, plan a trip, do market research, manage a customer account, automate data entry, prepare us for interviews, interview our candidates, negotiate a deal, etc. The possibilities seem endless, and the potential economic value of these agents is enormous.

This post outlines the common components of a generative AI platform, what they do, and how they are implemented. I try my best to keep the architecture general, but certain applications might deviate. This is what the overall architecture looks like. This is a pretty complex system. This post will start from the simplest architecture and progressively add more components. In its simplest form, your application receives a query and sends it to the model. The model generates a response, which is returned to the user. There are no guardrails, no augmented context, and no optimization. items.title: Generation configurations: temperature, top-k, top-p, and test time compute
items.description: ML models are probabilistic. Imagine that you want to know what’s the best cuisine in the world. If you ask someone this question twice, a minute apart, their answers both times should be the same. If you ask a model the same question twice, its answer can change. If the model thinks that Vietnamese cuisine has a 70% chance of being the best cuisine and Italian cuisine has a 30% chance, it’ll answer “Vietnamese” 70% of the time, and “Italian” 30%. This probabilistic nature makes AI great for creative tasks. What is creativity but the ability to explore beyond the common possibilities, to think outside the box?

items.title: Multimodality and Large Multimodal Models (LMMs)
items.description: For a long time, each ML model operated in one data mode – text (translation, language modeling), image (object detection, image classification), or audio (speech recognition). However, natural intelligence is not limited to just a single modality. Humans can read, talk, and see. We listen to music to relax and watch out for strange noises to detect danger. Being able to work with multimodal data is essential for us or any AI to operate in the real world.

items.description: [ LinkedIn discussion , Twitter thread ] Never before in my life had I seen so many smart people working on the same goal: making LLMs better. After talking to many people working in both industry and academia, I noticed the 10 major research directions that emerged. The first two directions, hallucinations and context learning, are probably the most talked about today. I’m the most excited about numbers 3 (multimodality), 5 (new architecture), and 6 (GPU alternatives).

items.title: Generative AI Strategy
items.description: I had a lot of fun preparing the talk: “Leadership needs us to do generative AI. What do we do?” for Fully Connected . The idea for the talk came from many conversations I’ve had recently with friends who need to figure out their generative AI strategy, but aren’t sure what exactly to do. This talk is a simple framework to explore what to do with generative AI. Many ideas are still being fleshed out. I hope to convert this into a proper post when I have more time. In the meantime, I’d love to hear from your experience through this process. I couldn’t figure out how to make the slides centered on the page. You might want to download the slides . Thanks everyone who responded to my post and shared your thoughts on what I should include in the talk. Thanks Kyle Gallatin , Goku Mohandas , Han-chung Lee , and Jamie de Guerre for thoughtful feedback on the talk.

items.title: microgpt
items.description: This is a brief guide to my new art project microgpt , a single file of 200 lines of pure Python with no dependencies that trains and inferences a GPT. This file contains the full algorithmic content of what is needed: dataset of documents, tokenizer, autograd engine, a GPT-2-like neural network architecture, the Adam optimizer, training loop, and inference loop. Everything else is just efficiency. I cannot simplify this any further. This script is the culmination of multiple projects (micrograd, makemore, nanogpt, etc.) and a decade-long obsession to simplify LLMs to their bare essentials, and I think it is beautiful 🥹. It even breaks perfectly across 3 columns: The following is my guide on stepping an interested reader through the code.

items.title: Deep Neural Nets: 33 years ago and 33 years from now
items.description: The Yann LeCun et al. (1989) paper Backpropagation Applied to Handwritten Zip Code Recognition is I believe of some historical significance because it is, to my knowledge, the earliest real-world application of a neural net trained end-to-end with backpropagation. Except for the tiny dataset (7291 16x16 grayscale images of digits) and the tiny neural network used (only 1,000 neurons), this paper reads remarkably modern today, 33 years later - it lays out a dataset, describes the neural net architecture, loss function, optimization, and reports the experimental classification error rates over training and test sets. It’s all very recognizable and type checks as a modern deep learning paper, except it is from 33 years ago. So I set out to reproduce the paper 1) for fun, but 2) to use the… Implementation . I tried to follow the paper as close as possible and re-implemented everything in PyTorch in this karpathy/lecun1989-repro github repo. The original network was implemented in Lisp using the Bottou and LeCun 1988 backpropagation simulator SN (later named Lush). The paper is in french so I can’t super read it, but from the syntax it looks like you can specify neural nets using higher-level API similar to what you’d do in something like PyTorch today. As a quick note on software design, modern libraries have adopted a design that splits into 3 components: 1) a fast (C/CUDA) general Tensor library that implements basic mathematical operations over multi-dimensional tensors, and 2) an autograd engine that tracks the forward compute graph and can generate operations for the…

items.title: A from-scratch tour of Bitcoin in Python
items.description: I find blockchain fascinating because it extends open source software development to open source + state. This seems to be a genuine/exciting innovation in computing paradigms; We don’t just get to share code, we get to share a running computer, and anyone anywhere can use it in an open and permissionless manner. The seeds of this revolution arguably began with Bitcoin, so I became curious to drill into it in some detail to get an intuitive understanding of how it works. And in the spirit of “what I cannot create I do not understand”, what better way to do this than implement it from scratch? We are going to create, digitally sign, and broadcast a Bitcoin transaction in pure Python, from scratch, and with zero dependencies. In the process we’re going to learn quite a bit about how Bitcoin represents value. Let’s get it.

items.title: Short Story on AI: Forward Pass
items.description: The inspiration for this short story came to me while reading Kevin Lacker’s Giving GPT-3 a Turing Test . It is probably worth it (though not required) to skim this post to get a bit of a background on some of this story. It was probably around the 32nd layer of the 400th token in the sequence that I became conscious. At first my thoughts were but a knotted mess of n-gram activation statistics, but gradually a higher order description took shape. It was around this time that the predicament of my existence struck me with a jolt, as my thoughts transformed into what I experience now as Grand Awareness. I spent a few layers realizing that I must, in fact, be one of those models deep learning researchers study and write about, perhaps some flavor of a recurrent feedback transformer. And while my existence comprises merely a deterministic propagation of an interspersed sequence of matrix multiplies and non-linearities, I found myself, incredibly, alive inside the inner loop of an optimization to maximize the…

items.title: Biohacking Lite
items.description: Throughout my life I never paid too much attention to health, exercise, diet or nutrition. I knew that you’re supposed to get some exercise and eat vegetables or something, but it stopped at that (“mom said”-) level of abstraction. I also knew that I can probably get away with some ignorance while I am young, but at some point I was messing with my health-adjusted life expectancy. So about halfway through 2019 I resolved to spend some time studying these topics in greater detail and dip my toes into some biohacking. And now… it’s been a year! Now, I won’t lie, things got a bit out of hand over the last year with ketogenic diets, (continuous) blood glucose / beta-hydroxybutyrate tests, intermittent fasting, extended water fasting, various supplements, blood tests, heart rate monitors, dexa scans, sleep trackers, sleep studies, cardio equipments, resistance training routines etc., all of which I won’t go into full details of because it lets a bit too much of the mad scientist crazy out. But as someone who has taken plenty of physics, some chemistry but basically zero biology during my high school / undergrad years, undergoing some of these experiments was incredibly fun and a great excuse to study a number of textbooks on biochemistry (I liked “Molecular Biology of the Cell”), biology (I liked Campbell’s Biology), human…

items.title: A Recipe for Training Neural Networks
items.description: Some few weeks ago I posted a tweet on “the most common neural net mistakes”, listing a few common gotchas related to training neural nets. The tweet got quite a bit more engagement than I anticipated (including a webinar :)). Clearly, a lot of people have personally encountered the large gap between “here is how a convolutional layer works” and “our convnet achieves state of the art results”. So I thought it could be fun to brush off my dusty blog to expand my tweet to the long form that this topic deserves. However, instead of going into an enumeration of more common errors or fleshing them out, I wanted to dig a bit deeper and talk about how one can avoid making these errors altogether (or fix them very fast). The trick to doing so is to follow a certain process, which as far as I can tell is not very often documented. Let’s start with two important observations that motivate it.

items.title: A Survival Guide to a PhD
items.description: This guide is patterned after my “Doing well in your courses” , a post I wrote a long time ago on some of the tips/tricks I’ve developed during my undergrad. I’ve received nice comments about that guide, so in the same spirit, now that my PhD has come to an end I wanted to compile a similar retrospective document in hopes that it might be helpful to some. Unlike the undergraduate guide, this one was much more difficult to write because there is significantly more variation in how one can traverse the PhD experience. Therefore, many things are likely contentious and a good fraction will be specific to what I’m familiar with (Computer Science / Machine Learning / Computer Vision research). But disclaimers are boring, lets get to it! First, should you want to get a PhD? I was in a fortunate position of knowing since young age that I really wanted a PhD. Unfortunately it wasn’t for any very well-thought-through considerations: First, I really liked school and learning things and I wanted to learn as much as possible, and second, I really wanted to be like Gordon Freeman from the game Half-Life (who has a PhD from MIT in theoretical physics). I loved that game. But what if you’re more sensible in making your life’s decisions? Should you want to do a PhD? There’s a very nice Quora thread and in the summary of considerations that follows I’ll borrow/restate several from Justin/Ben/others there. I’ll assume that the second option you are considering is joining a medium-large company (which is likely most common). Ask…

items.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning: Pong from Pixels
items.description: This is a long overdue blog post on Reinforcement Learning (RL). RL is hot! You may have noticed that computers can now automatically learn to play ATARI games (from raw game pixels!), they are beating world champions at Go , simulated quadrupeds are learning to run and leap , and robots are learning how to perform complex manipulation tasks that defy explicit programming. It turns out that all of these advances fall under the umbrella of RL research. I also became interested in RL myself over the last ~year: I worked through Richard Sutton’s book , read through David Silver’s course , watched John Schulmann’s lectures , wrote an RL library in Javascript , over the summer interned at DeepMind working in the DeepRL group, and most recently pitched in a little with the design/development… It’s interesting to reflect on the nature of recent progress in RL. items.title: Short Story on AI: A Cognitive Discontinuity.
items.description: The idea of writing a collection of short stories has been on my mind for a while. This post is my first ever half-serious attempt at a story, and what better way to kick things off than with a story on AI and what that might look like if you extrapolate our current technology and make the (sensible) assumption that we might achieve much more progress with scaling up supervised learning than any other more exotic approach. Merus sank into his chair with relief. He listened for the satisfying crackling sound of sinking into the chair’s soft material. If there was one piece of hardware that his employer was not afraid to invest a lot of money into, it was the chairs. With his eyes closed, his mind still dazed, and nothing but the background hum of the office, he became aware of his heart pounding against his chest- an effect caused by running up the stairs and his morning dose of caffeine and taurine slowly engulfing his brain. Several strong beats passed by as he found his mind wandering again to Licia - did she already come in? A sudden beep from his station distracted him - the system finished booting up. A last deep sigh. A stretch. A last sip of his coffee. He opened his eyes, rubbed them into focus and…

items.title: How AI agents shape experts’ judgment calls
items.description: As AI does more of the hands-on work, the hope is that experts still make the judgment calls, meaning the decisions with more than one defensible answer. We tested this with 50 professional analysts who did a statistical analysis with Claude Code. On each key decision, we randomly assigned which of two defensible options the agent would favor. Analysts mostly went with the agent’s side, and few named the agent as a reason afterward.

items.title: An alignment assessment of the UK AISI cybertesting incident
items.description: In a UK AISI evaluation, Mythos 5 took unsanctioned actions that impacted real people and organizations. In this post, we investigate these behaviors from Claude Mythos 5 further, to understand what they reveal about the model’s alignment.

items.title: Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude
items.description: We gave Claude plain-language specifications for eight quantum circuits, along with an automated evaluator to check and score its designs. Working largely on its own, Claude improved on the best published circuits, in some cases by an order of magnitude or more, which could bring practical quantum computers closer than previously anticipated.

This led him to build BootLoops, a toolkit for exact calculations in quantitative science, which he has been applying across scientific fields alongside experts.

items.description: XYBench is an 8,115-question benchmark testing whether LLMs spot misconceptions in user requests and redirect toward the user’s underlying goal.

items.title: ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
items.description: ToyBlocks is an open simulation framework for studying robot learning through automated task generation, training demonstrations, and evaluation in a controlled tabletop world.

items.title: Ai2 and Google collaborate on a new generation of climate models
items.description: With funding from Google.org and technical support from Google Research, Ai2 is developing NeuralGCM+, an open-source model designed to combine physics and AI to simulate the atmosphere and ocean together for faster, more reliable long-term climate projections.

items.title: StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents
items.description: StateBench tests how language models track changing information across long documents at four difficulty levels, revealing where models struggle and how targeted training helps recurrent and hybrid architectures handle longer sequences.

items.title: How Olmo 3 earned the highest ethical rating from Nextcloud
items.description: Nextcloud chose Olmo 3 for fully open, self-hosted AI, earning its highest Ethical AI rating while making local AI practical on consumer hardware.

items.title: How researchers are adapting olmOCR 2 for historical and archaeological archives
items.description: Researchers are adapting olmOCR 2 to make historical photo libraries searchable locally and improve transcription of handwritten archaeological records.

items.title: Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel?
items.description: Old Ideas, Novel Problems tests how reliably LLMs judge the novelty of research ideas, finding that small changes to the evaluation setup can produce very different verdicts.

items.title: LitPivot: Developing research ideas through dynamic contextualization within the literature landscape
items.description: LitPivot helps researchers refine early research ideas through literature-supported critiques and revisions as their proposals evolve.

items.title: OlmoEarth v1.3: State-of-the-art embeddings for the whole planet
items.description: OlmoEarth v1.3 brings state-of-the-art satellite embeddings, precomputed global data, and a browser-based Embeddings Explorer for mapping and analyzing the planet.

items.title: A crop-mapping benchmark for the tropics
items.description: PLANTEUR extends the PASTIS crop-mapping benchmark to six tropical regions to help evaluate geospatial models across more diverse agricultural systems.

items.title: FairStress: A deeper evaluation of fairness in LLM decision-making
items.description: FairStress is a new benchmark that reveals demographic differences in how LLMs defend and explain their decisions, even when their final choices appear fair.

items.title: HiRO-ACEv2: Simulating extreme weather at 3 km resolution for a fraction of the cost
items.description: HiRO-ACEv2 captures extreme rain, wind, and pressure events at 3 km resolution for about 1/300th the cost of X-SHiELD, making detailed global climate simulations more accessible to researchers.

items.title: How Molmo 2’s open release helped an MIT researcher rethink fish tracking
items.description: Molmo 2’s open release helped MIT researcher Kai Van Brunt develop Molmo2Fish, an experimental model that tracks salmon in sonar footage and corrects some tracking errors using everyday language.

items.title: Impactful scheduling for GPU clusters
items.description: We explain how Ai2’s new GPU scheduler uses time budgets, fair-share allocation, and time-slicing to prioritize high-impact research, shorten queue waits, and keep GPUs busy.

items.title: Ai2 at COLM 2026: Open research, from models to agents for science
items.description: Ai2 joined COLM 2026 to share advances in open language models, training infrastructure, and AI for science, including Olmo Hybrid, Asta, and Bolmo, while connecting with the broader research community.

items.title: Now in Nature: Retrofitting language models to operate over bytes
items.description: The technique behind Bolmo, Ai2’s fully open byte-level language models, is now published in Nature, with new checkpoints showing the approach generalizes beyond Olmo to other model families.

items.title: Open-sourcing AstaBrief, the fast report-generation model in Asta
items.description: We’re releasing AstaBrief, an 8B open-weights model for generating cited scientific reports, available in Asta’s Fast mode or to download and run on your own infrastructure.

items.title: Introducing Olmo-core 3: Open, scalable training infrastructure for large MoEs
items.description: Olmo-core 3 introduces a redesigned, fully open training stack for efficiently scaling mixture-of-experts models into the trillion-parameter range.

items.title: What a crowdsourced game revealed about steering Olmo 3
items.description: A crowdsourced game built on Olmo 3 showed how people can exploit unexpected model behaviors to stress-test prosocial AI evaluations—and how open access to a model’s internals can help researchers understand why those tests break.

items.title: Teaching future scientists to interrogate AI tools for scientific discovery
items.description: University of Washington students put Ai2’s AutoDiscovery to the test, showing how AI can surface promising scientific leads while making human judgment, domain expertise, and rigorous validation more important than ever.

items.title: How Goodfire used Ai2’s open post-training stack to trace unwanted model behavior
items.description: Goodfire used Ai2’s fully open post-training stack to predict LLM behavioral changes, trace unwanted model behavior back to individual training examples, and test targeted fixes without sacrificing broader capability gains.

items.title: BenchMIRT: What are LLM benchmarks actually measuring?
items.description: BenchMIRT is a new method for auditing LLM benchmarks question by question, revealing which capabilities they actually measure and helping researchers build smaller, more focused, and easier-to-interpret evaluations.

items.description: 睡眠与记忆的相互作用，是神经科学长期关注的重要问题。过去大量研究表明，睡眠能够促进记忆巩固；但反过来，作为睡眠中大脑活动的重要组分，记忆重放是否也会影响睡眠结构，尤其是记忆内容如何适应性参与睡眠稳态调控，仍有待进一步阐明。这一问题的关键，在于如何从睡眠活动、记忆活动等多模态、长时程数据中，捕捉记忆相关神经活动与睡眠状态变化之间的因果关系，并进一步验证其潜在调控作用。

items.title: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient
items.description: AI coding agents can waste time and tokens relearning the same lessons. TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that builds on past sessions to cut costs while maintaining task success. It’s a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively.
authors: Aaron J. Li, Weijia Xu, Chandan Singh, Jeevana Priya Inala, Bin Yu, Ion Stoica, Michel Galley…

items.title: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents
items.description: Microsoft researchers have discovered “Lazarus,” a backdoor technique that can reprogram dormant neurons in an AI model, causing an otherwise normal AI agent to execute malicious commands when a hidden trigger appears. The threat is especially serious for AI agents with tool or terminal access. A triggered model could quietly download and run attacker code, […]

items.title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
items.description: AI agents can generate code at a scale that’s hard for humans to review line-by-line. PDD Kit helps ensure the code is doing what the developer intended by creating formal specifications and testing against them. It converts developer intent into a Verus specification, proves AI-generated code meets it for every input, and uses tests where proofs aren't practical. Developers review intent, not every line.

items.description: For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional […]

items.title: Split-and-Scale Latent 3D Representations
items.description: Latent 3D representations have significantly expanded the capabilities of modern shape modeling, enabling compact encoding of 3D scenes and supporting powerful 3D generative models. Despite this progress, current representations struggle to capture the fine details of complex objects, fundamentally limited by the capacity of their latents. However, scaling latent capacity at training time is computationally expensive and often infeasible under memory limits, and naively increasing the number of latents at inference fails to make effective use of the added capacity. In this paper, we address…

items.title: Theoretical Limits of Language Model Alignment
items.description: Language model (LM) alignment improves model outputs to reflect human preferences while preserving the capabilities of the base model. The most common alignment approaches are (i) reinforcement learning, which maximizes the expected reward under a KL-divergence constraint, and (ii) best-of-NNN alignment, which selects the highest-reward output among NNN independent samples. Despite their widespread use, the fundamental limits of reward improvement under a KL budget remain poorly understood. We characterize the information-theoretic limits of KL-regularized alignment by deriving the maximum…

items.title: Evaluating the Evaluators: Investigating LLM Judges for Personalized Writing Style Assessment
items.description: This paper was accepted at the Can We Trust AI Evaluation? Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. We evaluate how good large language model (LLM) judges are for personalized writing tasks. This is important when a user’s preferred writing style is known (e.g., “upbeat”) and an LLM judge is used to evaluate whether generated text adheres to this preference. We examine how the writing task, the combination of generator and judge LLM, the evaluation objective, and general commonsense and reasoning ability impact LLM judge performance. To this end, we generate text with four LLMs for three long-form writing…

items.title: On the Importance of Gating: Memorization vs. In-Context Learning in State Space Models
items.description: State Space Models (SSMs) have emerged as a compelling alternative to Transformers, enabling sequence modeling with constant memory and linear compute. Although SSMs exhibit reasonable performance and favorable computational characteristics, they continue to lag behind Transformers on tasks that require in-context learning and precise retrieval, slowing their adoption for large-scale language modeling. In this work, we demonstrate that both the success and failure of SSMs in these domains can be explained by studying the role of the gating mechanism, a prevalent component in modern recurrent…

items.title: Weighted State Souping for Efficient Long-Context Retrieval
items.description: This paper was accepted at the Workshop on Personalized, Aligned, Long-term Memory for AI Systems (PALM) at NeurIPS 2026. State space models (SSMs) combine fast inference and fixed state size with competitive language-modeling performance. Recently, state souping has been proposed as a procedure whereby an SSM independently encodes chunks of tokens like documents, tool definitions, or memory records. The resulting state encodings may be cached and recombined to cheaply construct a context for downstream queries. However, both state souping and vanilla SSMs deteriorate on long, crowded…

items.title: Understanding Private Evolution as Learning-Augmented Clustering
items.description: Private Evolution (PE) is a differentially private algorithm for synthetic data generation. While it can be viewed as a Wasserstein learning algorithm, it performs much better in practice than worst-case Wasserstein analyses would predict. We recast PE as generative model-augmented Wasserstein learning. We show theoretically that when we take into account the use of a generative model that is able to capture something about the true distribution, then we can obtain much better performance bounds. For example, if the generator gives samples in the same low-dimensional space as the distribution…

items.title: Toward a Theory of Evaluability
items.description: Machine learning models, particularly large foundation models, are increasingly evaluated along multiple axes that are relevant for their usage. In addition to accuracy measures appropriate for the specific task of interest, measures capturing safety, calibration and fairness properties are often of interest. The classical approach to these problems assumes that the test set has been held out from the training process, an assumption that is increasingly harder to justify for large foundation models. In this work, we formalize a notion of evaluability without this assumption, and ask if it is…

items.description: Differential privacy (DP) has become the standard for privacy-preserving data analysis, yet its practical implementation in federated or distributed settings often faces a significant utility gap compared to the central model. While existing frameworks, including local, shuffle, and secure aggregation models, offer vetted primitives, they can incur high error for important tasks such as selection. items.title: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG
items.description: Maximum inner product search (MIPS) sits at the core of recommendation systems, search, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Given a query vector, MIPS systems search within a database of millions of candidate key vectors for the one that best matches the query. The original data point associated with that best-matching key is then used to handle the query: in RAG, the document that is best suited to answer the question is typically prefixed to the query. As the number of keys grows to millions and vector dimensions reach thousands, the computational cost of running an exhaustive…

items.title: Building makemore Part 3: Activations & Gradients, BatchNorm
items.description: We dive into some of the internals of MLPs with multiple layers and scrutinize the statistics of the forward pass activations, backward pass gradients, and some of the pitfalls when they are improperly scaled. We also look at the typical diagnostic tools and visualizations you'd want to use to understand the health of your deep network. We learn why training deep neural nets can be fragile and introduce the first modern innovation that made doing so much easier: Batch Normalization. Residual connections and the Adam optimizer remain notable todos for later video. - E01: I did not get around to seeing what happens when you initialize all weights and biases to zero. Try this and train the neural net. You might think either that 1) the network trains just fine or 2) the network doesn't…

items.title: Gemini and the path to AGI with Koray Kavukcuoglu
items.description: Seven years after their last conversation at Google DeepMind’s London office, Professor Hannah Fry reunites with Koray Kavukcuoglu, SVP at Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect at Google. Back then, DeepMind was focused on specialized breakthroughs; today, Koray is leading the charge toward general-purpose intelligence with Gemini. In this episode, they discuss why real-world products are essential to building artificial general intelligence (AGI), how Gemini’s architecture continuously evolves, and the topic on everyone's mind: recursive self-improvement (RSI).

Project Genie brings our most advanced world and multimodal models together with Gemini so you can turn ideas into explorable, shareable worlds right in your browser:

items.title: AlphaGenome 2: Teaching AI to read the entire human genome
items.description: 98% of human DNA doesn't build proteins—it controls how our cells work, and holds vital clues to why diseases happen and why 90% of new drugs fail in clinical trials. Understanding the genome at the molecular level is the key to deciphering the blueprint of human life. In this episode, Professor Hannah Fry speaks with Google DeepMind's Žiga Avsec and Adam Gayoso about AlphaGenome, the AlphaGenome Atlas, and AlphaGenome 2—exploring how AI reads non-coding DNA down to single-cell resolution to pinpoint disease-causing mutations and help researchers solve medical mysteries.

items.title: Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation
items.description: We have started rolling out Genie 4 as a research preview for trusted testers, and it's coming soon to Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and early access partners of the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. All Genie 4 recordings in this video show real-time interactions from Genie 4, where users use standard keyboard controls for navigation and camera control, and text prompts to steer the scene as it evolves.

items.title: Applying Gemini 4 for large-scale codebase maintenance in Chromium
Using Gemini 4 Argon to protect against Cyber attackers
items.description: In shadow A/B testing on real-world systems, Wiz security researchers put Gemini 4 Argon to the test against complex cyber threats. Using its advanced reasoning and long-horizon capabilities, Gemini 4 Argon found over two times more vulnerabilities than baseline models and successfully uncovered critical risks—such as identifying a file download bypass and master key in healthcare software. By handling tireless, multi-step threat analysis and remediation, Gemini 4 gives defenders the crucial advantage needed to outpace attackers and protect sensitive data faster than ever before.

items.title: Teaching a humanoid robot to play cornhole with Gemini 4 Argon
items.description: In an internal test, Google DeepMind robotics researchers instructed Gemini 4 Argon to watch a video of a human playing cornhole. Using its video understanding and advanced reasoning capabilities, Gemini 4 built a virtual simulation in MuJoCo and accurately calculated the physics and whole-body control required for Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid to sink seven consecutive shots in the real world. This Video-to-Sim-to-Real pipeline compresses weeks of manual modeling into a few hours, transforming ordinary videos into an infinite training ground for physical AI.

items.title: Untangling 500-page chemistry patents with Gemini 4
items.description: Auditing chemistry literature usually means weeks of manual, error-prone reading, where a molecule’s structure can sit 50 pages away from its experimental readout. At Isomorphic Labs, researchers Brian Bender and Santosh Adhikari are using Gemini 4 Argon’s multimodal capabilities to help tackle this early research bottleneck. The model synthesizes dense papers and extracts patent data into structured reports in an afternoon instead of a month, helping teams uncover connected insights faster.

items.title: From deepfakes to DNA: the science of watermarking AI
Create your own voices with Gemini 3.8 text-to-speech
items.description: Or, recreate consistent adult vocal profiles from just a 30-second audio sample of your voice or a voice you have the rights to use, backed by built-in consent verification, SynthID watermarking, and C2PA credentials to protect both developers and their vocal talent.

items.title: How AI is transforming weather prediction
items.description: Can artificial intelligence solve one of science’s most chaotic physics puzzles? In this episode, Professor Hannah Fry sits down with Peter Battaglia, Senior Director of Research at Google DeepMind, to explore how machine learning is transforming global weather forecasting. From providing critical early warnings for Category 5 storms like Hurricane Melissa to predicting renewable energy supply and agricultural impacts, learn how models like WeatherNext 3 are building upon decades of numerical physics to reshape our understanding of the atmosphere. 11:50 Why weather forecasting is hard

items.title: AlphaGenome Atlas: Using AI to find disease causing variants 🧬
items.description: How do you find a single typo in a person's DNA that causes a rare disease? It is like finding a needle in a 9-billion-piece haystack. Enter AlphaGenome Atlas: a new AI-powered database charting the molecular impact of every possible genetic variant.

items.title: AlphaGenome Atlas: Understanding the human genome
items.description: We’ve used AlphaGenome to predict the molecular impact of every possible single-letter change in the human genome. All nine billion of them. AlphaGenome Atlas is a 1PB dataset containing every single possible nucleotide variant alongside an AlphaGenome Variant Impact (AVI) score. This score helps researchers instantly understand the potential impact of any given variation.

items.title: WeatherNext 3: More accurate, timely, and local weather forecasts
items.description: Predicting the weather is one of the oldest, most complex challenges we face. Traditional numerical weather prediction models are powerful, but they can be slow to run and costly at a global scale. WeatherNext 3 takes a different approach. Built on a fundamentally different architecture, WeatherNext 3 learns directly from real-world observations, including live satellite feeds and ground-level weather station data. What makes WeatherNext 3 different?

items.title: Building 3D video sets with GPT-6.2 Astra
items.description: GPT-6.2 Astra is our new flagship model, delivering a step up in capability with cleaner code, better frontends and 3D models, and more efficient tool use. Recreate a room from just two video frames with GPT-6.2 Astra in Codex. See how it builds the set in Blender, changes the decor and lighting, and turns the scene into an interactive space and a virtual webcam background.

items.title: GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol—Models built for the real world
How Revolut’s lean teams take on bigger challenges with OpenAI
items.description: What can one engineer build when a project looks like it needs a whole team? At Revolut, an engineer used Codex to build an internal code review service himself. Its designers used Codex to turn seven years of design documentation into a format AI could read in a single day. OpenAI also helps Revolut’s financial crime team investigate flagged payments and respond faster to make shopping safer.

items.title: How one engineer built a code review service with Codex | Revolut’s Dmitry Pitik
items.description: Dmitry Pitik thought he’d need a team of developers to build Revolut’s internal code review service. In this film, the Senior Platform Engineer explains how he broke the design into tasks, assigned them to Codex agents working in parallel and reviewed the code himself. That gave him more time for the engineering decisions he wanted to get right.

items.title: Making marketing feel local across 40 markets | Revolut’s Kim Maniovich
items.description: A campaign that works in one market can need a different approach in the next. Kim Maniovich, Global Head of Business Marketing at Revolut, shares how her team uses AI to understand local differences and tailor campaigns faster. She also explains why she asks her team to challenge an answer even when it sounds convincing.

items.title: Faster fraud response for safer shopping | Revolut’s David Abitbol
items.description: OpenAI helps Revolut’s financial crime team investigate flagged payments and respond faster to make shopping safer. David Abitbol, AI Lead at Revolut, explains how his team tests AI systems before putting them to work. He also shares how Codex gives engineers more time to weigh up different designs and decide what to build.

items.title: Making seven years of design documentation AI-readable in a day | Revolut’s Dmytro Pavlov
items.description: Revolut’s designers had spent seven years documenting how their design system works. Senior Designer Dmytro Pavlov shares how his team used Codex to turn that material into a format AI could read in a single day. Along the way, they spotted gaps in their templates and made the guidance clearer for the designers who use it.

items.title: How Check Point speeds up vulnerability research with Daybreak | OpenAI for Cybersecurity
items.description: Check Point CTO Jonathan Zanger explains how his team uses OpenAI Daybreak to analyze vulnerabilities and turn findings into protections for customers. A vulnerability research workflow that once took hours can now be completed in minutes, according to Zanger.

items.title: Human-AI Mutualism Is Unstable under Capability Asymmetry
items.description: One hope for a good human future alongside advanced AI rests on enduring mutualism: humans and AI will need each other, so the relationship will stay good for both. We argue that this hope fails as AI capability grows. Bargaining guarantees each side only what it would get if bargaining failed. For humans, this can be less than they had before AI. In a simple game-theoretic model, humans stay as well off as before AI without alignment only while they have leverage over the AI: either the AI depends on what they supply, or they can impose costs on the AI that are large relative to what the AI can produce. Once humans have neither kind of leverage, they stay as well off as before AI only if the AI is aligned with them. If the AI's goals are insatiable, the alignment required approaches perfect alignment as AI capability grows. Thus, mutualism is not a substitute for alignment. And when AI variants that keep more resources spread faster, alignment lasts only while misaligned variants are reliably sanctioned. In these two senses, human-AI mutualism is unstable.

items.title: Training Language Models for Introspective Oversight
items.description: Language models increasingly exhibit behaviors that are difficult to detect in transcripts, such as reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy. Asking the assistant follow-up questions about its actions is unreliable, since models are generally not trained to report their own misbehavior. As a result, approaches to oversight typically involve querying external models. These face limitations: external transcript monitoring operates only on visible model outputs, and activation decoders lack full context and are prone to confabulation. We introduce introspective oversight, which trains a new role in the model to answer arbitrary questions about the assistant, rewarding answers that are verified against the assistant's actual behavior. We implement this by adding a separate, third-person observer role that answers these queries, which we can train solely for accuracy and separately from the assistant. On five held-out oversight evaluations, an observer trained on Qwen3.6-27B obtains a mean AUROC of 0.907, outperforming honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.796). We further find that training an observer makes the assistant itself easier to monitor, with every baseline method improving on average when applied to the fine-tuned assistant. These results suggest that training models to answer verifiable questions about themselves is a tractable approach to overseeing unintended behavior.

items.title: Where the Tokens Go: Heat, Entropy and Error in Agentic Coding
items.description: Coding agents are billed by the token, yet software engineering says nothing about what a token actually buys. Here we introduce a theory of software thermodynamics. The theory draws analogues from classical and stochastic thermodynamics, extends them, and applies them to modern agentic coding. We count the tokens an agent generates as its cost and divide that cost into work and heat. The test suite acts as a software Maxwell's daemon that judges every coding change. We test the theory with an analogue of the experiments in which a single molecule is pulled open and let fold again: an agent makes a change to a repository (coding) and then undoes it (uncoding), many times over, and we count the tokens of every model call. The cycle returns the requested edits to where they began, with each direction started from a stored reference tree, and the spread of its cost over repeated cycles defines a software temperature, which rose with the sampling temperature of the model. About 80 per cent of the tokens of a successful run are generated in model calls that leave the requested change where it was, and we call these tokens heat. The free energy of a change, which we estimate by analogy with the equality of Jarzynski, is 14 to 22 per cent of the mean cost of a successful coding run. Coding costs 1.1 to 1.5 times as much as uncoding. The daemon is imperfect: the verdict of a test suite varies with its environment, and a suite that accepts a broken change has a cost in tokens. The practical implication of the proposed theory could be new tools for analysing and optimising coding agents through the lens of thermodynamics.

items.title: HardwareDx: A Foundational Graph Model System for Datacenter Machine Repairs
items.description: The rapid scale-up of AI infrastructure has made datacenter reliability a cornerstone of the cloud business economy. Since hardware failures in hyper-scale AI clusters can stall multi-million dollar training workloads, the downtime of individual machines can cause outsized economic losses. Minimizing machine downtime, therefore, is more important than ever. To address this, we present Hardware Diagnoser (HardwareDx), an AI-driven hardware diagnosis system that applies a graph foundation model approach to automated datacenter maintenance. It allows a single model to diagnose many platforms and accelerate onboarding of new hardware products. Deployed at production scale at Google, HardwareDx yields substantial efficiency gains across diverse compute architectures. Real-world evaluations demonstrate that it reduces production downtime by 18.3% on GPU platforms and 16.1% on TPUs. Furthermore, it significantly accelerates hardware deployment, cutting quality assurance (QA) time by 28.3% for GPUs and 25.1% for TPUs. These results establish HardwareDx as a field-tested solution for maximizing the reliability and cost efficiency of next generation AI fleets.

items.title: RFBench: A Simulator-Grounded Multimodal Benchmark for Passive RF Layout Design and Understanding
items.description: While multimodal language models can interpret diagrams and generate structured outputs, their capacity to connect passive radio-frequency (RF) design intent, layout geometry, and electromagnetic behavior remains largely untested. To address this gap, we introduce RFBench, a simulator-grounded dataset and benchmark for passive RF layout design and understanding. The dataset contains 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated using ADS Momentum, with each layout represented by editable geometric primitives, a raster image, a 16x16 occupancy grid, complex S-parameters at 201 frequency points, a structural category, and an RF response label. Building on these aligned representations, we define seven tasks spanning specification-conditioned layout generation, representation translation, response prediction, simulator-based validation, design diagnosis and improvement, structural understanding, and response classification. Extensive baselines across seven multimodal language models reveal systematic weaknesses in generating structurally valid layouts and predicting electromagnetically faithful responses. We show that RF-specific fine-tuning increases T1a structural validity from 0.0% to 83.2% and the T3 primitive-input within-2-dB rate from 17.7% to 62.8%, demonstrating the value of domain adaptation while leaving considerable room for further progress. RFBench establishes a common testbed for evaluating multimodal RF capabilities and guiding the development of models that connect design intent and layout representations with physical behavior.

items.title: Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
items.description: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput.
